relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: The prophetic community admits its home has become too small.
They propose labor, timber, and shared building by Jordan.
Presence is requested along with permission.
Teacher and students go together to work.
A borrowed tool disappears into water, and the poor worker cries out.
The lost iron is restored at the exact place of failure.
The worker must still reach out and take it.
War councils whisper in hidden rooms.
The prophet's warning keeps Israel from the trap.
Repeated attention prevents repeated loss.
The enemy king mistakes prophetic insight for betrayal.
A servant names Elisha as the one hearing the hidden chamber.
The king sends force to capture one voice.
Night surrounds Dothan with horses and chariots.
The servant sees danger first and asks what can be done.
Fear is answered with a wider horizon.
The mountain becomes visible as full of fiery protection.
The attacking force loses reliable perception.
Elisha leads the disoriented army into the city it meant to attack.
Their eyes open in the middle of Samaria.
The king immediately asks permission to kill.
Elisha rejects execution and commands bread and water.
A feast becomes the unexpected weapon that halts raids for a time.
Later, the larger machinery of war returns as siege.
Samaria's market becomes a measure of starvation.
A woman calls to the king from below the wall.
The king confesses the emptiness of royal rescue.
Her grief opens into an agreement formed under impossible hunger.
One child has been eaten; the other is hidden.
The king tears his clothes, and sackcloth is revealed beneath power.
His grief seeks a head to blame.
Elisha recognizes the execution order before it arrives.
The king names catastrophe as Divine and loses patience with waiting.

contemplative_note: This chapter moves from a borrowed axe to a starving city. Its clearest ethical miracle is not spectacle but restraint: captives who could have been killed are fed and sent home. Siege later returns, proving mercy is not magic—but it remains mercy.
